results.quote: The answer this chapter gives is that a shop holds one person in many systems for different purposes.
results.finding: flowA 3.1: 'the thesis is stated about three times before the case starts' (KEY POINTS, ¶1's conclusion, ¶2, then the roadmap). The spec places the thesis in both the callout and p05 after p01's map conclusion, so the repetition comes from the declared intro structure.
results.corroborated_by: flowB 3.1 ('The opening says the same thing three times')

results.quote: Next come the lawful bases and consent, including consent at a store's till; retention and the split of the person from the transaction; a request across many systems; and the requirements of the four privacy flows side by side.
results.finding: flowA 3.1: the roadmap sentence 'is too long to hold, and I had to re-read it'; it also names 'the four privacy flows' before they are identified.
results.corroborated_by: flowB 3.2 (same sentence; 'four privacy flows' have not been named; could not hold the roadmap)

results.quote: The chapter's case is a different customer with a longer history.
results.finding: flowA 3.2: Eva's paragraph 'comes after the roadmap and just before the case, introduces Eva, then drops her at once'. The spec places p04 after the roadmap; both readers suggest moving it before the roadmap or cutting it.
results.corroborated_by: flowB 3.3 / 2.1 (Eva paragraph out of place between roadmap and scene)

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Request From Ghent ¶4
results.quote: Outside those nine systems, the newsletter tool, one of the shop platform's apps, unsubscribed her through the shop platform's notification;
results.finding: flowA 3.3: nine systems plus the newsletter tool plus the iPaaS 'makes eleven systems that held her, yet the text says she was "in nine of the thirteen systems"'; the OMS sentence before it is also unexplained here.
results.corroborated_by: flowB 3.4 and 3.5 (nine or eleven; the OMS sentence has no reason given)

results.draft_locus: What Personal Data a Commerce Platform Holds, and Under Which Rules ¶1
results.quote: Lotte's request used words that carry the design: controller, the one-month limit, records that must be kept.
results.finding: flowA 3.4: 'Lotte's request did not use these words. The narration of the scene did.'
results.corroborated_by: flowB 3.6 (her request was 'delete my data and stop emailing me')

results.quote: such as the Dutch or Belgian one above
results.finding: flowA 3.5: 'No Dutch or Belgian regulator has appeared above. They first appear later, in the Consent section.'

results.quote: That clock runs in hours from the breach; it is separate from the one-month clock for a person's request, which comes later in the chapter.
results.finding: flowA 3.6: the breach-notification paragraph 'is a different topic from sharing and transfers ... it still feels parked here'. The spec deliberately puts the breach clock in the vendor paragraph of Sharing and Transfers.
results.corroborated_by: flowB 3.12 (breach clock tucked into 'The vendor's side', interrupts the sharing line)

results.quote: Whatever the rules become, consent has to be asked well where it is asked.

results.quote: consent capture and consent withdrawal (in the consent section), the retention purge (in the retention section)

'The identity rule' and 'the July matching run' (terms 23; flowA 3.14, flowB 3.18) are on already_knows (chapter 27's June 2027 identity rule), so they are not new to the declared audience. The right of withdrawal and the prior-price rule are forward pointers to the next chapter. Controller, processor, DPA, lawful basis, DSR, retention, consent, soft opt-in, cookie walls, CMP, server-side tagging, pseudonymization, identity index, orchestrator, action table, backup exception, adequacy, SCCs, DPF, transfer inventory and the breach clock are each defined where first needed in the body.

The introduction opens on a bridge from the previous chapter and a concrete removal scenario, then states a specific, disputable answer; no weak opening pattern. The repeated thesis is recorded under flow.
The conclusion opens by answering the opening case with three causes and one remedy, not by restating section titles, and ends on questions and a hand-off.

What to Take Away ¶1 joins the roles, the person-on-the-order and the missing index into three reasons and one map, and gives the so-what: the second request took two working days with a record a regulator asks for.
¶1 returns to the request from Ghent ('took seventeen working days for three reasons') and to Eva's order, and says what made the second request take two, as conclusion.callback asks.

The intro reader predicted the copies across systems, the map of roles, actions and retention, the request reaching every system, the section order matching the roadmap, Eva's order, and the evidence (Kestrel & Pine's nine-system request and autumn 2027 design, GDPR and ePrivacy, EDPB, Dutch and Belgian regulators, national retention rules, Shopify's documentation).

The reader rejects deleting the web-shop account, cites nine of thirteen systems, and gives verification, the identity index, per-system erase/pseudonymize/retain, referral of bol, carrier and PSP, the backup exception with log replay, the one-month-plus-two reply saying what was erased, kept and whom to ask, and the record.

The reader explains the retention periods as a legal obligation, the invoice-as-customer-record conflict that deletes nothing, and the split (reference and delivery address on the order, erasable profile, hashed analytics, retention per record type with a scheduled purge).

The reader covers consent before device access except the cart and language, no cookie walls, scrolling or pre-ticked boxes, the soft opt-in with free objection subject to national rules, consent recorded per person and purpose with time, place, wording and source on the master reaching tags, newsletter, POS and apps, same-day withdrawal, no-consent default when the CMP is down, the store sign-up rule and server-side tagging not removing the need for consent.
